name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ENVIRONMENTALISSUES_MATCHING_Q01 - Pollution control devices and target pollutants

questiontext.text:
Match the pollution control devices or methods in Column I with the pollutants or wastes they address in Column II.

Column IColumn II
(a) Catalytic converter(i) Particulate matter
(b) Electrostatic precipitator(ii) Carbon monoxide and nitrogen oxides
(c) Earmuffs(iii) High noise level
(d) Sanitary landfills(iv) Solid wastes

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Different environmental pollutants—gaseous automobile emissions, industrial particulates, high-intensity noise, and municipal trash—require specific control technologies.

Step 2: Matching Each Item
1. A catalytic converter fitted into automobiles uses platinum-palladium and rhodium catalysts to convert poisonous gases such as carbon monoxide and nitric oxide into carbon dioxide and nitrogen gas, matching (a) with (ii).
2. An electrostatic precipitator removes over \(99\%\) of particulate matter from thermal power plant exhaust, matching (b) with (i).
3. Earmuffs are personal protective devices used to muffle and protect ears from high noise levels, matching (c) with (iii).
4. Sanitary landfills are trenches where compacted solid wastes are dumped and covered with dirt daily, matching (d) with (iv).

Step 3: Verification of Pairings
Each control measure corresponds uniquely to its target pollutant: catalytic converter \(\rightarrow\) carbon monoxide and nitrogen oxides; electrostatic precipitator \(\rightarrow\) particulate matter; earmuffs \(\rightarrow\) high noise level; sanitary landfills \(\rightarrow\) solid wastes.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The correct matching is (a)-(ii), (b)-(i), (c)-(iii), (d)-(iv).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ENVIRONMENTALISSUES_MATCHING_Q02 - Environmental acts and international treaties with years

questiontext.text:
Match the environmental acts and international treaties in Column I with their respective years of enactment or signing in Column II.

Column IColumn II
(a) Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act(i) 1981
(b) Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act(ii) 1987
(c) Environment (Protection) Act(iii) 1974
(d) Montreal Protocol (signed)(iv) 1986

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Legislative measures in India and international treaties were enacted at specific milestones to safeguard water, air, overall environment, and the stratospheric ozone layer.

Step 2: Matching Each Item
1. The Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act was passed by the Government of India in 1974 to safeguard water resources, matching (a) with (iii).
2. The Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act came into force in India in 1981 (and was later amended in 1987 to include noise), matching (b) with (i).
3. The Environment (Protection) Act was passed in 1986 to protect and improve the quality of air, water, and soil, matching (c) with (iv).
4. The Montreal Protocol was signed at Montreal, Canada in 1987 (effective in 1989) to control emission of ozone-depleting substances, matching (d) with (ii).

Step 3: Verification of Pairings
Chronological order of enactment/signing: Water Act (1974) \(\rightarrow\) Air Act (1981) \(\rightarrow\) Environment Protection Act (1986) \(\rightarrow\) Montreal Protocol (1987).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The correct matching is (a)-(iii), (b)-(i), (c)-(iv), (d)-(ii).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ENVIRONMENTALISSUES_MATCHING_Q03 - Constituents of domestic sewage and waterborne diseases

questiontext.text:
Match the categories of impurities or contaminants in domestic sewage in Column I with their examples or effects in Column II.

Column IColumn II
(a) Suspended solids(i) Nitrate, ammonia, phosphate, sodium, calcium
(b) Colloidal material(ii) Sand, silt and clay
(c) Dissolved materials(iii) Dysentery, typhoid, jaundice, cholera
(d) Pathogenic micro-organisms(iv) Fecal matter, bacteria, cloth and paper fibres

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A mere \(0.1\%\) of impurities makes domestic sewage unfit for human use. These impurities are classified into suspended solids, colloidal materials, dissolved materials, and pathogenic micro-organisms.

Step 2: Matching Each Item
1. Suspended solids in wastewater include sand, silt, and clay, matching (a) with (ii).
2. Colloidal material consists of fecal matter, bacteria, cloth, and paper fibres, matching (b) with (iv).
3. Dissolved materials include nutrients and salts such as nitrate, ammonia, phosphate, sodium, and calcium, matching (c) with (i).
4. Disposal of untreated sewage containing pathogenic micro-organisms from homes and hospitals causes outbreaks of serious diseases like dysentery, typhoid, jaundice, and cholera, matching (d) with (iii).

Step 3: Verification of Pairings
Physical state classification confirms: sand/silt/clay are suspended; fecal matter/fibres are colloidal; ions/nutrients are dissolved; and pathogens cause infectious diseases.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The correct matching is (a)-(ii), (b)-(iv), (c)-(i), (d)-(iii).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ENVIRONMENTALISSUES_MATCHING_Q04 - Aquatic pollution phenomena and ecological concepts

questiontext.text:
Match the terms related to water pollution in Column I with their correct descriptions in Column II.

Column IColumn II
(a) Eichhornia crassipes(i) Increase in toxicant concentration at successive trophic levels
(b) Biomagnification(ii) Estimate of biodegradable organic matter in sewage water
(c) Cultural eutrophication(iii) 'Terror of Bengal', blocks waterways in eutrophic waters
(d) Biochemical Oxygen Demand(iv) Radical acceleration of lake aging by nitrates and phosphates

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Nutrient enrichment, organic waste, and persistent industrial toxicants trigger distinct ecological phenomena in aquatic ecosystems.

Step 2: Matching Each Item
1. Eichhornia crassipes (water hyacinth) is the world's most problematic aquatic weed, called the 'Terror of Bengal', which grows abundantly in eutrophic water bodies and blocks waterways, matching (a) with (iii).
2. Biomagnification refers to the increase in concentration of a non-metabolisable toxicant (such as DDT or mercury) at successive trophic levels, matching (b) with (i).
3. Cultural or accelerated eutrophication is the radical acceleration of a lake's natural aging process caused by human pollutants like nitrates and phosphates from sewage and agricultural/industrial wastes, matching (c) with (iv).
4. Biochemical Oxygen Demand (BOD) is measured to estimate the amount of biodegradable organic matter present in sewage water, matching (d) with (ii).

Step 3: Verification of Pairings
All four pairs align directly with the definitions and ecological roles described for aquatic pollution.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The correct matching is (a)-(iii), (b)-(i), (c)-(iv), (d)-(ii).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ENVIRONMENTALISSUES_MATCHING_Q05 - Environmental case studies, pioneers, and initiatives

questiontext.text:
Match the individuals, groups, or systems in Column I with their associated environmental initiatives in Column II.

Column IColumn II
(a) Ahmed Khan(i) Upkeep of six connected marshes for wastewater treatment in California
(b) Ramesh Chandra Dagar(ii) Developed Polyblend mixed with bitumen to lay roads in Bangalore
(c) Friends of the Arcata Marsh (FOAM)(iii) Dry composting toilets recycling human excreta in Kerala and Sri Lanka
(d) EcoSan toilets(iv) Integrated organic farming and Haryana Kisan Welfare Club

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Innovative, sustainable solutions to plastic waste, agro-chemical pollution, wastewater treatment, and human excreta disposal have been demonstrated through successful community and individual case studies.

Step 2: Matching Each Item
1. Ahmed Khan, a plastic sack manufacturer in Bangalore, developed Polyblend (recycled modified plastic powder) and proved that blending it with bitumen enhances water-repellent properties and triples road life, matching (a) with (ii).
2. Ramesh Chandra Dagar, a farmer in Sonipat, Haryana, practices integrated organic farming (combining bee-keeping, dairy management, water harvesting, composting, and agriculture) and founded the Haryana Kisan Welfare Club, matching (b) with (iv).
3. Friends of the Arcata Marsh (FOAM) is a citizens' group responsible for the upkeep and safeguarding of the integrated wastewater treatment project involving six connected marshes in Arcata, California, matching (c) with (i).
4. EcoSan toilets are working dry composting toilets in many areas of Kerala and Sri Lanka that recycle human excreta into natural fertiliser, matching (d) with (iii).

Step 3: Verification of Pairings
Each pioneer or system corresponds uniquely to its geographic location and sustainable innovation.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The correct matching is (a)-(ii), (b)-(iv), (c)-(i), (d)-(iii).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ENVIRONMENTALISSUES_MATCHING_Q06 - Auto fuel policy and Euro III fuel specifications

questiontext.text:
Match the fuel emission parameters in Column I with their stipulated limits under the auto fuel policy / Euro III norms in Column II.

Column IColumn II
(a) Euro III sulphur limit in diesel(i) \(150\text{ ppm}\)
(b) Euro III sulphur limit in petrol(ii) \(50\text{ ppm}\)
(c) Euro III aromatic hydrocarbons limit in fuel(iii) \(350\text{ ppm}\)
(d) Roadmap goal for sulphur in petrol and diesel(iv) \(42\text{ per cent}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The Government of India's auto fuel policy lays out a roadmap to cut vehicular pollution by steadily reducing sulphur and aromatic hydrocarbon content in petrol and diesel.

Step 2: Matching Each Item
1. Euro III norms stipulate that sulphur be controlled at \(350\text{ parts-per-million (ppm)}\) in diesel, matching (a) with (iii).
2. Euro III norms stipulate that sulphur be controlled at \(150\text{ ppm}\) in petrol, matching (b) with (i).
3. Under Euro III norms, aromatic hydrocarbons are to be contained at \(42\text{ per cent}\) of the concerned fuel, matching (c) with (iv).
4. According to the roadmap, the goal is to reduce sulphur to \(50\text{ ppm}\) in both petrol and diesel (and bring aromatic hydrocarbons down to \(35\text{ per cent}\)), matching (d) with (ii).

Step 3: Verification of Pairings
Diesel has a higher initial sulphur limit (\(350\text{ ppm}\)) than petrol (\(150\text{ ppm}\)) under Euro III, while the roadmap target lowers both to \(50\text{ ppm}\), and aromatic hydrocarbons are capped at \(42\%\) under Euro III.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The correct matching is (a)-(iii), (b)-(i), (c)-(iv), (d)-(ii).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ENVIRONMENTALISSUES_MATCHING_Q07 - Greenhouse gases and stratospheric ozone concepts

questiontext.text:
Match the atmospheric terms in Column I with their correct values or descriptions in Column II.

Column IColumn II
(a) Carbon dioxide(i) Unit for measuring thickness of ozone column
(b) Methane(ii) \(60\%\) contribution to total global warming
(c) Dobson unit (DU)(iii) Inflammation of cornea caused by high dose of UV-B
(d) Snow-blindness(iv) \(20\%\) contribution to total global warming

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Global warming and stratospheric ozone depletion are two major global atmospheric issues with distinct contributing gases, measurement units, and biological effects.

Step 2: Matching Each Item
1. Carbon dioxide contributes \(60\%\) to total global warming, matching (a) with (ii).
2. Methane contributes \(20\%\) to total global warming, matching (b) with (iv).
3. The thickness of ozone in a column of air from the ground to the top of the atmosphere is measured in Dobson units (DU), matching (c) with (i).
4. In the human eye, the cornea absorbs UV-B radiation, and a high dose causes inflammation of the cornea called snow-blindness, matching (d) with (iii).

Step 3: Verification of Pairings
Carbon dioxide (\(60\%\)) and methane (\(20\%\)) are the top two greenhouse gas contributors; DU measures ozone thickness; snow-blindness is a UV-B-induced corneal inflammation.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The correct matching is (a)-(ii), (b)-(iv), (c)-(i), (d)-(iii).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ENVIRONMENTALISSUES_MATCHING_Q08 - Forest conservation movements and policies in India

questiontext.text:
Match the forest conservation events and policies in Column I with their correct details in Column II.

Column IColumn II
(a) Amrita Devi Bishnoi (1731)(i) Local women hugging trees in Garhwal Himalayas
(b) Chipko Movement (1974)(ii) Recommended \(33\%\) forest cover for plains and \(67\%\) for hills
(c) Joint Forest Management (1980s)(iii) Sacrificed life protecting trees near Jodhpur, Rajasthan
(d) National Forest Policy (1988)(iv) Government-community partnership sharing forest products

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
People's participation and government policies have played a central role in forest conservation in India.

Step 2: Matching Each Item
1. In 1731, Amrita Devi, a Bishnoi woman near Jodhpur in Rajasthan, hugged a tree to stop the king's men from cutting it and sacrificed her life along with her daughters and hundreds of Bishnois, matching (a) with (iii).
2. In 1974, the Chipko Movement in the Garhwal Himalayas saw local women bravely protecting trees from contractors' axes by hugging them, matching (b) with (i).
3. In the 1980s, the Government of India introduced Joint Forest Management (JFM) to work closely with local communities for protecting and managing forests in return for forest products like fruits, gum, rubber, and medicine, matching (c) with (iv).
4. The National Forest Policy (1988) of India recommended \(33\%\) forest cover for the plains and \(67\%\) for the hills, matching (d) with (ii).

Step 3: Verification of Pairings
All four events and policies match their respective years, regions, and conservation mechanisms.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The correct matching is (a)-(iii), (b)-(i), (c)-(iv), (d)-(ii).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ENVIRONMENTALISSUES_MATCHING_Q09 - Hazardous, solid, electronic, and radioactive waste disposal

questiontext.text:
Match the categories of wastes in Column I with their recommended treatment or disposal methods in Column II.

Column IColumn II
(a) Hospital hazardous waste(i) Environment-friendly recycling to recover copper, iron, silicon, nickel, and gold
(b) Biodegradable solid waste(ii) Disposal using incinerators
(c) Electronic waste (e-waste)(iii) Shielded containers buried within rocks about \(500\text{ m}\) deep
(d) Radioactive nuclear waste(iv) Placed in deep pits in the ground for natural breakdown

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Different waste streams—biomedical, biodegradable organic, electronic, and radioactive—pose distinct hazards and require tailored disposal or recovery methods.

Step 2: Matching Each Item
1. Hospitals generate hazardous wastes containing disinfectants, harmful chemicals, and pathogenic micro-organisms; the use of incinerators is crucial for their disposal, matching (a) with (ii).
2. Biodegradable solid wastes can be put into deep pits in the ground and left for natural breakdown, matching (b) with (iv).
3. Electronic wastes (irreparable computers and electronic goods) contain recoverable metals like copper, iron, silicon, nickel, and gold; environment-friendly recycling is the only proper solution, matching (c) with (i).
4. After sufficient pre-treatment, radioactive nuclear waste is recommended to be stored in suitably shielded containers buried within rocks about \(500\text{ m}\) deep below Earth's surface, matching (d) with (iii).

Step 3: Verification of Pairings
Each waste type is paired with its specific, chapter-prescribed disposal or recovery protocol.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The correct matching is (a)-(ii), (b)-(iv), (c)-(i), (d)-(iii).
